definition:
Prayer is speech addressed to God by people who believe he hears. In Scripture it is never a technique for bending the divine will or a monologue with oneself; it is the answer of creatures to a God who has already spoken, made promises, and bound himself to his people. The Bible's prayers cover the full range of human speech: praise for who God is, thanksgiving for what he has done, confession of sin, petition for oneself, intercession for others, and lament, the complaint of a believer who brings grief, anger, and confusion to God instead of away from him. Jesus teaches his disciples to call God “Father” (Luke 11:2), the New Testament teaches that believers pray through Christ, who intercedes for them (Hebrews 7:25), and in the Spirit, who helps them when “we do not know how we ought to pray” (Romans 8:26). Christian prayer is therefore shaped by the Trinity: to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.

The Hebrew vocabulary is broad. The usual verb for praying is hitpallēl (from the root pll), with the noun tĕpillâ, ‘prayer’; the Psalms end one of their collections with the note, “Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse” (Psalm 72:20). People also ‘call’ (qārāʾ) on the name of the LORD, ‘cry out’ (ṣāʿaq or zāʿaq) in distress, ‘seek’ (bāqaš, dāraš) God's face, and make ‘supplication’ (tĕḥinnâ, a plea for favor). Praise has its own words: hālal, ‘to praise’, from which comes hallelujah, ‘praise the LORD’, and yādâ, ‘to give thanks’ or ‘to confess’, since thanksgiving in Israel was public acknowledgment of what God had done. The Greek New Testament uses proseuchomai and proseuchē for prayer in general, deomai and deēsis for specific requests, aiteō for ‘asking’, eucharisteō for ‘giving thanks’, and entygchanō, ‘to appeal’ or ‘intercede’, for the Spirit's and Christ's intercession (Romans 8:27, 34; Hebrews 7:25). 1 Timothy 2:1 strings four of these together (petitions, prayers, intercessions, thanksgiving), less as a technical classification than as a way of saying ‘every kind of prayer’. Lament is not a single Hebrew word but a kind of psalm, identified by its shape: address, complaint, petition, and usually a turn to trust or praise.
ot:
People begin to pray early in the story. After Cain's murder of Abel and the birth of Seth, Genesis notes that “At that time men began to call upon the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26). The patriarchs build altars and call on God's name (Genesis 12:8), and their prayers are startlingly frank. Abraham bargains for Sodom, appealing to God's own justice, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25), while confessing that he is “but dust and ashes” (Genesis 18:27). Jacob, afraid of Esau, prays God's promises back to him (Genesis 32:9-12) and then wrestles through the night, refusing to let go without a blessing (Genesis 32:26). In Egypt the enslaved Israelites simply groan, and “God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant” (Exodus 2:24). The exodus itself begins as the answer to a cry. After the golden calf Moses intercedes for the people, reminding God of his promises and his reputation among the nations, and “the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened” (Exodus 32:14). That passage shows two things the rest of Scripture keeps together: God is not manipulated, and yet he has chosen to act in response to the prayers of his servants.

Israel's worship gave prayer a place and a pattern. The priests blessed the people in God's name (Numbers 6:24-26), and Hannah, barren and mocked, poured out her soul at the sanctuary at Shiloh so silently that the priest Eli thought she was drunk (1 Samuel 1:10-15). Samuel told Israel that to stop praying for them would be a sin against the LORD (1 Samuel 12:23). At the dedication of the temple Solomon prayed that God, whom “Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain” (1 Kings 8:27), would hear every prayer made toward that house, by Israelites in trouble, by sinners who repent, by a foreigner who comes for God's name's sake, and by exiles in a far land (1 Kings 8:27-53). The temple was a meeting place for prayer, not a container for God, and Isaiah foresaw that it would “be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (Isaiah 56:7), a line Jesus quoted when he cleared the temple courts (Mark 11:17). In exile, where there was no temple, prayer carried the faith. Jeremiah's letter promised the exiles that God would listen when they sought him with all their heart (Jeremiah 29:12-13); Daniel prayed three times a day toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10); and the great prayers of confession in Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, and Daniel 9 plead for mercy, not “because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion” (Daniel 9:18).

The Psalms are Israel's prayer book, and the church's. They teach prayer by giving words to pray: hymns of praise, songs of thanksgiving, royal psalms, wisdom psalms, psalms of trust, and more laments than any other kind. The form-critical study of Hermann Gunkel and later Claus Westermann classified these types, and Walter Brueggemann's The Message of the Psalms (1984) popularized a reading of them as songs of orientation, disorientation, and new orientation. The laments are the Bible's great surprise. They ask “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1), accuse God of absence, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), and in Psalm 88 end in darkness without any turn to praise. Yet they are prayers. They argue with God because they believe his promises, and most move from complaint to trust: “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion” (Psalm 13:5). Psalm 51 gives the Bible its classic confession, and Psalm 62 invites the whole people to “pour out your hearts before Him” (Psalm 62:8). Some psalms call down judgment on enemies (Psalms 35, 69, 109, 137); they hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it, and interpreters differ on how Christians should pray them.

Lament does not end with the Psalms. Jeremiah complains that God has deceived him (Jeremiah 20:7-18), Habakkuk asks “How long, O LORD, must I call for help” (Habakkuk 1:2) and receives an answer that calls for patient faith, and Lamentations, five poems over the ruins of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, holds grief and hope side by side, confessing that the LORD's mercies are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22-23) and then closing on an unresolved plea (Lamentations 5:20-22). Job's speeches are prayer at the edge of faith, and God's final verdict is that Job, who had spoken to him in protest, spoke rightly, while his friends, who had spoken about him in pious generalities, did not (Job 42:7). Jonah prays from the belly of the fish (Jonah 2), and his book ends with God questioning a prophet who resents mercy for Nineveh. The Old Testament leaves a clear picture: prayer is covenant speech, honest to the point of protest, grounded in God's promises, and answered in God's own time and way.
nt:
Jesus prayed, and the Gospels take care to show it. He rose while it was still dark to pray alone (Mark 1:35), withdrew often to the wilderness to pray (Luke 5:16), and spent a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12). Luke especially places prayer at the turning points: at his baptism (Luke 3:21), at the transfiguration (Luke 9:28-29), and on the cross. When the disciples asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1), he gave them the prayer Christians call the Lord's Prayer, in a shorter form in Luke 11:2-4 and a longer one in Matthew 6:9-13. It begins with God's name, kingdom, and will before it asks for bread, forgiveness, and deliverance, and it teaches disciples to address God as ‘Father’ together, ‘our Father’. The closing doxology familiar from church use (‘for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory’) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts of Matthew, such as Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, though an early form of it appears in the Didache; this is why many modern Bibles, including the BSB, print it only in a footnote.

Jesus' teaching on prayer is simple and demanding. Prayer is not performance: “go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen” (Matthew 6:6). It is not heaping up words, “for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him” (Matthew 6:8). Yet the Father who knows still wants to be asked: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7), for if human fathers give good gifts, “how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him” (Luke 11:13). He told parables about persistence, a friend at midnight (Luke 11:5-8) and a widow wearing down an unjust judge, told so that his hearers would “pray at all times and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). And he warned that prayer can be a vehicle of pride: the Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other men, while the tax collector, beating his breast, prays “God, have mercy on me, a sinner” and goes home justified (Luke 18:9-14). In John's Gospel Jesus promises that prayer in his name will be answered (John 14:13-14), and asking in his name means asking as those who belong to him and seek what he seeks.

Jesus' own prayers show what his teaching meant. In Gethsemane he asked for the cup to pass, and then submitted: “Yet not what I will, but what You will” (Mark 14:36). Hebrews says he “offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). On the cross he prayed Psalm 22, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34), taking Israel's lament into his own mouth; he prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and he died with the words of Psalm 31:5 (Luke 23:46). His longest recorded prayer, in John 17, is intercession for his disciples and for all who would believe through them, “that all of them may be one” (John 17:21). After his resurrection and ascension that intercession continues: he “always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). This is the ground of Christian boldness: because the great high priest sympathizes with human weakness, believers may “approach the throne of grace with confidence” (Hebrews 4:16).

The early church was a praying community. The disciples waited for the Spirit “With one accord” in prayer (Acts 1:14); the first believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42); and when threatened, they prayed not for safety but for boldness, and the place was shaken (Acts 4:24-31). The church prayed fervently for Peter in prison (Acts 12:5). Paul's letters are full of prayer reports and requests, and his instructions are sweeping: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17); pray about everything with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will guard hearts and minds (Philippians 4:6-7); pray for rulers and all in authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2). He teaches that the Spirit enables believers to cry “Abba” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6), the Aramaic word Jesus used in Gethsemane, and that the Spirit “intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26) when believers themselves cannot find words. Paul also knew unanswered prayer: three times he asked for his thorn in the flesh to be removed and was told instead, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

The later letters apply this to ordinary life. James says believers lack because they do not ask, or ask with wrong motives (James 4:2-3); he tells the sick to call the elders to pray and anoint them, commends mutual confession, and says that “The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (James 5:16), pointing to Elijah, “a man just like us” (James 5:17). Peter tells his readers to cast all their anxiety on God “because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). John assures them that God hears whatever they ask “according to His will” (1 John 5:14). Revelation gathers the church's prayers into heavenly worship: golden bowls of incense “which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8), the martyrs' lament “How long, O Lord” (Revelation 6:10), and the Bible's last prayer, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20).

keyTexts.why: Abraham intercedes for Sodom, appealing to God's justice with boldness and humility. The first extended prayer of intercession in the Bible.
Moses pleads God's promises and name for a guilty people, and the LORD relents. A key text for how prayer relates to God's purposes.
Hannah pours out her soul in silent, weeping prayer. Prayer as honest distress brought before God.
Solomon's temple prayer asks God to hear every prayer made toward his house, including the foreigner's and the exile's.
A short lament that moves from ‘How long, O LORD?’ to trust in God's loving devotion. The shape of lament in miniature.
A cry of abandonment that turns to praise. Jesus prays its opening words from the cross.
The Bible's classic prayer of confession, appealing to God's loving devotion and compassion for cleansing.
An exile's prayer of confession for his people, asking mercy on the ground of God's compassion, not Israel's righteousness.
Jesus warns against prayer as performance or many words and gives the Lord's Prayer.
The disciples ask to be taught to pray; Jesus gives the prayer, a parable of persistence, and the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit.
Two parables: the persistent widow, and the Pharisee and the tax collector. Prayer without losing heart and without pride.
Jesus in Gethsemane asks for the cup to pass and submits to the Father's will. The pattern of honest request and surrender.
The Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes with groans too deep for words.
Because Jesus is a sympathetic high priest, believers may approach the throne of grace with confidence.
The prayers of the saints rise before God with incense, and the judgments that follow answer them.

history:
The church inherited its patterns of prayer from Israel: set hours, the Psalms, blessings over food, and prayer toward a holy place. The Didache, an early Christian manual usually dated to the late first or early second century, instructs believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. The first Christian treatises on prayer came soon after: Tertullian's On Prayer (about 200), Origen's On Prayer (about 233), which takes up the objection that prayer is pointless if God foreknows everything, and Cyprian of Carthage's On the Lord's Prayer (about 252). In the monastic movement prayer became the center of an ordered life. John Cassian, writing in his Conferences in the early fifth century, taught the constant repetition of the opening verse of Psalm 70 as a way to pray without ceasing, and the Rule of Benedict (about 530) organized the monastic day around the daily office, so that the whole Psalter was prayed each week. In the East, the tradition of hesychasm (from the Greek for ‘stillness’) centered on the Jesus Prayer, a short plea for mercy addressed to Christ, repeated in attentive stillness; Gregory Palamas defended it in the fourteenth century, and the Philokalia, a collection of Eastern writings on prayer, was published in 1782 by Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain and Makarios of Corinth.

The Reformers kept prayer central but reshaped it. They insisted that prayer be addressed to God alone through Christ the one mediator, and in the language of the people. Martin Luther wrote A Simple Way to Pray (1535) for his barber, Peter Beskendorf, teaching him to pray through the Lord's Prayer, the Ten Commandments, and the Creed. John Calvin devoted one of the longest chapters of his Institutes (Book 3, chapter 20) to prayer, calling it the chief exercise of faith. Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised 1552 and 1662) brought the daily office into English for ordinary parishes. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) calls prayer the most important part of the thankfulness God requires (question 116), and the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647) defines prayer and closes with an exposition of the Lord's Prayer (questions 98 to 107). Catholic spirituality after the Reformation produced Ignatius of Loyola's Spiritual Exercises (approved 1548) and Teresa of Ávila's Interior Castle (1577). English Puritans and later Free Church traditions pressed for extemporaneous prayer, and the dispute over set forms helped drive the ejection of some two thousand ministers who would not conform to the 1662 Prayer Book.

Theologians have also asked how prayer relates to God's sovereignty. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 83, article 2) taught that we do not pray in order to change God's plan, but to obtain what God has arranged to give through prayer, so that prayer is one of the causes God has ordained. The Reformed and much of the Lutheran and Catholic traditions follow a similar line. Arminian and Wesleyan theology stresses God's real responsiveness within his foreknowledge, and in the late twentieth century open theists such as Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, and Gregory Boyd argued that God has chosen not to fix every detail of the future and genuinely responds to prayer as events unfold. The site's pages on providence and on sovereignty and freedom set out these positions at length. In recent decades many writers have also recovered lament for the church's worship, after long neglect in many Western congregations.

differ.view: Prayer as a means God has ordained
differ.body: God's plan is eternal and complete, and prayer is not outside it but inside it. God has willed to accomplish many things through the prayers of his people, just as he has willed to feed people through farming. So prayer truly matters: without it the things God ordained to give in answer to prayer would not come. Moses' intercession (Exodus 32) and Elijah's prayers (James 5:17-18) are real causes within God's providence, and ‘the LORD relented’ describes God's action as experienced within history. Defenders include Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, John Calvin, and the Reformed and much of the Catholic tradition.

differ.view: Prayer as genuine influence on a responsive God
differ.body: Scripture presents God as truly hearing and answering, sometimes changing a stated course because of prayer (Exodus 32:14; 2 Kings 20:1-6). Arminian theologians affirm God's full foreknowledge while stressing that he takes human requests into account in his decisions. Open theists such as Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, and Gregory Boyd go further, holding that God has freely created a world in which the future is partly open, so that prayer makes a difference not already settled in advance. Both groups argue that this reading takes the Bible's narratives of divine response at face value and gives prayer its full urgency.

The Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that believers may ask the saints in heaven to pray for them, as they ask fellow believers on earth. The church is one family in Christ, living and departed, and the prayers of the righteous have great power (James 5:16); the saints in Revelation offer prayers before God (Revelation 5:8). Asking their intercession is not worship, which belongs to God alone, and it adds nothing to Christ's unique mediation but shares in it. The Council of Trent (1563) set out this teaching for Catholics, and Orthodox liturgy asks the prayers of the saints throughout its services.

differ.view: Prayer to God alone through Christ
differ.body: Protestant churches hold that Scripture gives no command or example of praying to the departed and that Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), who always lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25). The Augsburg Confession (1530, article 21) allows the saints to be remembered and imitated but not invoked. Believers are invited to approach the throne of grace directly (Hebrews 4:16), and asking the living to pray for one another is commanded, while addressing prayers to the saints risks giving creatures the trust that belongs to God.

errors:
The church has rejected prayer as magic, the idea that the right words, repeated enough or said with enough confidence, compel God. Jesus warned against babbling like the pagans who think they will be heard for their many words (Matthew 6:7), and the Bible's prayers submit their requests to God's will as Jesus did in Gethsemane. Modern forms of the same error include teaching that a believer can speak health or wealth into being by confident declaration, and that unanswered prayer always proves weak faith. Paul's thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7-9), Jesus' own prayer about the cup, and the psalms that end unanswered all stand against it. The opposite error is fatalism: since God has decided everything, prayer changes nothing and is merely therapy for the one who prays. Scripture never draws that conclusion; it commands asking and records answers.

The church has also rejected extremes about the place of prayer. The Messalians, condemned at a synod at Side (about 390) and at the Council of Ephesus (431), taught that unceasing prayer alone, not baptism or the sacraments, freed the soul from indwelling evil. Quietism, the teaching of Miguel de Molinos condemned by Pope Innocent XI in 1687, urged a passive state of soul in which even the desire for salvation should be abandoned. Other distortions are more ordinary: prayer used to display piety (Matthew 6:5), prayer that is all request and no praise or confession, prayer that suppresses lament as if honesty before God were unbelief, and prayer that asks God to act while refusing to act oneself (James 2:15-16).
life:
The Bible does not treat prayer as a skill that must be mastered before it can be done. Its first prayers are groans and cries, and the Spirit helps those who do not know what to say. Many Christians have found it steadying to pray the Psalms, since they give words for joy, guilt, fear, and rage that a person might not dare to say on his own, and to use the Lord's Prayer as both a prayer and a pattern: God's name, kingdom, and will first, then daily needs, forgiveness, and protection. Set times and set prayers are not the enemy of sincerity, and spontaneous prayer is not a lack of reverence; both traditions have fed believers for centuries.

Lament belongs in the life of prayer. People who are grieving, depressed, or angry at God often think they must pretend before him or stop praying, and the psalms show another way: bring the complaint to God, in words, and wait. Lament is not the absence of faith but faith that will not let go. Unanswered prayer remains a real trial; Scripture does not explain every case, but it shows Jesus praying ‘not as I will’ and Paul receiving grace instead of relief. For someone in crisis, prayer does not replace calling on others for help, and the same New Testament that commands prayer commands the church to bear one another's burdens. Prayer also turns outward: for enemies, for rulers, for the church, and for the world, in the confidence that the risen Christ intercedes, and in the hope voiced by the Bible's final prayer, ‘Come, Lord Jesus.’
questions: The Psalms include laments that accuse God of forgetting and forsaking. What does it mean that Scripture gives believers words like these to pray, and when have you needed them?
Jesus teaches persistence in prayer (Luke 18:1) and also prays ‘not what I will, but what You will’ (Mark 14:36). How do bold asking and submission to God's will fit together?
Christians differ on how prayer relates to God's sovereign plan. Whichever view you hold, what reasons does Scripture give to keep praying?
